name: Ohm's law lab
summary: Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance: V = I × R. You'll measure the voltage across and the current through four resistors, then compare each with its nominal (color-code) value. The difference is the deviation: 100 × (measured − nominal) / nominal. A big deviation means the wrong part or a wiring mistake.
source: Adapted from James M. Fiore, Laboratory Manual for DC Electrical Circuit Analysis, v1.4.3 (exercises 1, 3 and 4, and Appendix D), licensed CC BY-NC-SA. Follow your own course's handout if it differs.
safety: No food or drink at the bench: liquids are conductive.
Set the power supply to zero volts, output off, before you build or change the circuit.
Never connect the DMM in current mode directly across the supply: it blows the meter's fuse.
If a resistor gets hot or smells, turn the output off right away and tell your TA.
When you finish, leave the bench secure: sources at zero and all equipment off.

steps.title: Get set up
steps.instruction: Get your breadboard, test leads, the adjustable DC power supply, a digital multimeter, short 22 or 24 gauge hookup wire, and the four resistors: 220, 470, 1k and 2.2k ohms. Turn the supply's voltage down to zero.
steps.why: Starting at zero volts means nothing is live while you build. Thin solid hookup wire fits the breadboard without damaging it.

terms.DMM: Digital multimeter: measures DC voltage, current and resistance.
terms.Breadboard: A board with holes connected in groups of five underneath, so you can build circuits without soldering.
terms.Ohm: The unit of resistance. 1k means 1,000 ohms.

steps.checkpoint: All parts are at the bench and the supply is set to zero volts.

steps.title: Read the color codes
steps.instruction: Read each resistor's bands. The first two bands are digits, the third is how many zeros to add, and the fourth is tolerance: gold means plus or minus 5 percent. 220 is red, red, brown. 470 is yellow, violet, brown. 1k is brown, black, red. 2.2k is red, red, red. Line them up as resistor 1 to 4.
steps.why: Resistors look almost identical. The color code is the label, and mixing parts up is the most common reason a lab's numbers don't match.

terms.Color code: Black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. A memory trick: Black Bears Robbed Our Yummy Goodies Beating Various Gray Wolves.
terms.Tolerance: How far the real value may be from the nominal value. Gold is 5 percent, silver 10 percent.
terms.Nominal value: The value printed by the color code.

steps.checkpoint: Four resistors identified and lined up in order.

steps.title: Build the circuit with resistor 1
steps.instruction: Place resistor 1 so its two legs sit in two different five-hole rows. Wire the supply's positive lead to one leg. Set the DMM to DC current and insert it in-line between the other leg and the supply's negative lead, so the current flows through the meter.
steps.why: To measure current, the current has to pass through the meter, so it goes in series. Both legs in the same row would short the resistor out.

terms.In-line (series): Part of the single loop, so the same current flows through it.
terms.Row: Each group of five holes on a breadboard is connected inside.

steps.checkpoint: Resistor 1 spans two rows and the DMM is in-line in the loop.

steps.title: Raise the supply to 5 volts
steps.instruction: Turn the supply on with the voltage at zero and check the DMM reads zero current. Then slowly raise the supply to 5 volts.
steps.why: Starting from zero and raising it slowly lets you catch a wiring mistake before much current flows. At zero volts, Ohm's law predicts zero current.

terms.Volt: The unit of voltage, the push that drives current.

steps.checkpoint: The supply reads 5 volts and the DMM shows a current.

steps.title: Record the current
steps.instruction: Read the current on the DMM in milliamps and remember it, or say it to me.
steps.why: This is the measured current. Ohm's law predicts I = V / R, so we'll compare the two.

steps.title: Measure the voltage
steps.instruction: Turn the supply down to zero. Take the DMM out of the loop and reconnect the resistor straight to the supply's negative lead. Set the DMM to DC volts, raise the supply back to 5 volts, and touch the probes across the two ends of the resistor.
steps.why: Voltage is measured across a part, in parallel, not through it. The meter compares the two ends of the resistor.

terms.Across (parallel): Connected to both ends of the part, side by side with it.

steps.checkpoint: The DMM shows the voltage across resistor 1.

steps.title: Read your values to me
steps.instruction: Say the resistor number, the volts and the milliamps, like 'resistor 1, 4.98 volts, 22.4 milliamps'. I'll work out the resistance and the deviation and tell you if something's off. Then turn the supply to zero, swap in the next resistor, and repeat steps 3 to 6 for resistors 2, 3 and 4.
steps.why: Comparing measured and nominal values, with the percent deviation, is exactly what your lab report's data table asks for. A big deviation catches a wrong part or a wiring mistake right away.
